title: H-Row — は ひ ふ へ ほ

points.name: は
points.explanation: The syllable は combines 'h' with the vowel あ, producing a clear 'ha' sound as in 'hat' or 'happy'. Japanese 'h' is similar to English 'h' — a gentle, breathy sound produced by pushing air through an open throat. は is absolutely essential to learn not just as a sound, but because it doubles as the topic particle, one of the most important grammatical particles in Japanese. When you see は used as a particle (rather than part of a word), it's actually pronounced 'wa' — a well-known exception that every learner encounters early.
rules: As a syllable in words, は is pronounced 'ha'. As the topic particle, は is pronounced 'wa'.
The topic particle は marks what you're talking about: わたしはがくせいです means 'I am a student'.
は is written in three strokes and has a distinctive shape — don't confuse it with ほ.
points.flashcardAnswer: ha — like 'ha' in 'hat' (or 'wa' when used as the topic particle)

points.name: ひ
points.explanation: The syllable ひ pairs 'h' with the vowel い, producing a 'hi' sound like the English word 'he'. The 'h' in ひ is slightly more palatal than in は — your tongue naturally rises toward the palate when moving from 'h' to 'ee', giving ひ a slightly softer quality than the 'he' in 'hen'. ひ appears in key vocabulary including ひと (person / human being), ひ (fire / day / sun), and ひく (to pull / to play a stringed instrument). It also appears in the counting suffix: ひとつ means 'one thing'.
rules: The 'h' becomes slightly softer and more palatal before い — a natural result of the tongue position.
ひ appears in ひと (person) — one of the most fundamental Japanese nouns.
Watch for ひ vs ほ — they look similar with their horizontal elements, but ひ has the 'ee' vowel sound.

points.name: ふ
points.explanation: The syllable ふ is the most distinctive sound in the H-row — it's not quite 'fu' as in English 'food', and it's not 'hu' either. Japanese ふ is made by bringing both lips close together (bilabial) and letting air pass through, then adding the Japanese 'u' vowel. It's softer than English 'f' (which involves the upper teeth and lower lip) and sounds somewhere between 'fu' and 'hu'. Many Japanese learners describe it as a 'breathy f'. ふ appears in ふね (boat), ふたつ (two things), and the beloved greeting ふじさん (Mt. Fuji).
rules: Bring both lips slightly close together — don't use your upper teeth like in English 'f'.
The result is a soft, breathy sound between 'f' and 'h', unique to Japanese.
The 'u' vowel is unrounded (flat lips), making this sound noticeably different from English 'food'.
points.flashcardAnswer: fu — a soft bilabial 'f', unique to Japanese

points.name: へ
points.explanation: The syllable へ pairs 'h' with the vowel え, making a 'he' sound as in 'hen' or 'help'. Like は, the character へ has a special dual role: when used as the directional particle meaning 'toward' or 'to', it's pronounced 'e' (just the vowel, no 'h'). So にほんへいく (going to Japan) has the へ pronounced as 'e': 'Nihon e iku'. As a standalone syllable in words, however, へ keeps its full 'he' sound. The character へ is notable for its simplicity — it looks like a little mountain peak and is one of the easiest hiragana to write.
rules: In words, へ is 'he'. As the directional particle, へ is pronounced 'e' (the 'h' is silent).
The directional particle へ indicates movement toward a destination.
The character へ looks like a simple peak or mountain — one of the simplest hiragana shapes.

examples.english: (archaic form; へ as particle: にほんへ = to Japan)

points.flashcardAnswer: he — like 'he' in 'hen' (or 'e' when used as the directional particle)

points.name: ほ
points.explanation: The syllable ほ combines 'h' with the vowel お, making a 'ho' sound like the start of 'home' or 'hope'. ほ appears in high-frequency vocabulary: ほん (book), ほし (star), ほか (other / besides), and ほんとう (really / truly — often shortened to ほんと in casual speech). The character ほ looks quite similar to は — both have the same basic left structure, but ほ has an extra horizontal stroke at the top right. Learners sometimes mix these two up, so pay close attention to that distinguishing feature.
rules: Clean 'h' + pure 'oh' vowel, stopping cleanly without gliding to 'w'.
ほ looks similar to は — check carefully: ほ has an extra horizontal stroke that は doesn't.
ほん (book) and ほんとう (really) are extremely high-frequency words using ほ.

chapterPractice.prompt: What sound does は make when used as the TOPIC PARTICLE?
chapterPractice.explanation: When used as the topic particle, は is pronounced 'wa', not 'ha'. This is one of Japanese's most famous exceptions — the same character has two pronunciations depending on its function.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which character makes a unique bilabial sound between 'f' and 'h'?
chapterPractice.explanation: ふ makes the distinctive Japanese 'fu' sound — produced with both lips close together (bilabial), unlike English 'f' which uses teeth and lip. It's softer and breathier than English 'fu'.
はな (hana) means 'flower' or 'nose' — the same word for both! Context makes the meaning clear. は (ha) + な (na) = hana.
ひと (hito) means 'person' or 'human being'. ひ (hi) + と (to) = hito. This is one of the most fundamental Japanese nouns.
